h05.minimum_viable_analytic: Build a supplier-month E1399 misuse score using claims, beneficiary, provider, order, authorization, payment, and document-text data. Start with all P&O claims containing E1399 or custom-item modifiers, then join by claim line and beneficiary/date to the closest clinically comparable L-code family using HCPCS crosswalks, diagnosis/body-site fields, product descriptions, and same-beneficiary historical claims. Compute: E1399 share of P&O lines and allowed dollars; median and 90th-percentile E1399 allowed amount divided by the matched L-code allowance; percentage of claims with missing design, fabrication, labor, or material fields; percentage with generic order language; percentage with reused item features; and pairwise or locality-sensitive text similarity of construction narratives, flagging supplier-months with similarity above 0.90 or feature reuse above 80%. Add a documentation-completeness indicator based on linked design records, itemized costs, labor hours, raw-material entries, and delivery evidence. Standardize each feature against specialty- and geography-matched peer distributions using robust z-scores or percentile ranks. Produce a weighted score such as 25% payment-ratio percentile, 20% E1399 utilization percentile, 20% narrative-reuse percentile, 20% documentation-deficiency percentile, and 15% generic-order or linkage-deficiency percentile. Send the top-scoring supplier-months to manual review, sample both flagged and unflagged claims for validation, and suppress or adjust features when low volume, legitimate rare indications, or incomplete document feeds could create false positives.

h11.minimum_viable_analytic: Build a beneficiary-equipment episode table from Medicare Advantage or FFS claims, DME rental-month/payment history, enrollment, inpatient and HHA claims, prescription/order records where available, supplier and clinician NPIs, beneficiary address, HCPCS/modifiers, and equipment serial numbers. Normalize HCPCS into same-or-similar equipment groups; partition records by beneficiary and group; identify each prior rental or ownership event and its last paid rental month, then identify a subsequent rental start within 180 days. Compute features for each candidate reset: gap in days from last paid rental month or ownership event; distance from the applicable 60-day-plus-remaining-month threshold; prior paid rental months; same HCPCS/group indicator; same serial-number indicator; unchanged address, ordering clinician, diagnosis, and delivery channel; supplier-change indicator; presence and timing of inpatient, HHA, or voluntary nonbilling intervals; new-prescription indicator; reset-documentation completeness; and number of suppliers or NPIs involved. Score candidates with a transparent weighted rule or logistic model, for example assigning high weights to same serial number, same address and clinician, short or threshold-adjacent gaps, continuous diagnosis, and a prior rental history near completion, while treating corroborated clinical resolution and documented equipment return as mitigating factors. Aggregate candidate resets by supplier, ordering clinician, HCPCS group, and month; calculate reset rate per 1,000 rental episodes, median gap, proportion with only inpatient/nonbilling support, and paid months generated after reset. Compare each entity with specialty, geography, and beneficiary-mix peers using robust z-scores or percentile ranks; queue claims or suppliers when a candidate-level score and supplier-level outlier score both exceed policy thresholds. Preserve an auditable explanation record listing the exact claims and fields that generated each alert, and re-run the measures monthly to detect post-edit migration to new suppliers, clinicians, or documentation sources.

h28.minimum_viable_analytic: Use the claims warehouse, Medicare enrollment and provider files, beneficiary eligibility, encounter and E&M claims, DMEPOS order or CMN repositories, clinical-document metadata where available, supplier ownership and location data, and marketer or lead-source records where contractually available. Normalize ordering-provider identifiers, supplier NPIs, HCPCS codes into product families, ICD diagnoses into clinically meaningful groups, and service dates to a monthly grain. Create a base table with one row per beneficiary-order-supplier-month and compute: ordering-provider share of a supplier's beneficiaries and allowed claim volume; ordering-provider share by HCPCS family and diagnosis; supplier/provider HHI; order volume divided by the clinician's attributed Medicare patient count and E&M volume; telehealth encounter share; days from encounter to order signature and from signature to first claim; repeat diagnosis, length-of-need, accessory-combination, and narrative-template indicators; replacement-history conflicts; and cross-supplier, cross-state, shared-beneficiary, shared-address, shared-phone, ownership, and marketer link counts. For narrative fields, remove identifiers, dates, and common boilerplate, then calculate token n-gram or MinHash similarity within HCPCS-family and diagnosis cohorts, with a separate exact-template rate. Score each supplier-provider-month using a weighted percentile model: 25% concentration/HHI, 20% provider-to-clinical-activity ratio, 20% documentation similarity, 15% clinical-consistency failures, 10% rapid encounter-to-order-to-claim timing, and 10% cross-entity network connectivity. Calibrate thresholds against specialty, geography, product family, and legitimate high-volume provider peers; generate a beneficiary-level sample for record review and a provider-supplier network queue for SIU investigation. Require at least two independent signal families before adverse action and retain feature values, peer groups, and source records for reproducibility.

h17.minimum_viable_analytic: Build a beneficiary-supplier-item episode table from medical and DME claims, pharmacy-equivalent supply claims where available, eligibility/death data, hospice election, institutional admission, therapy-discontinuation and equipment-return records, prescription/order and renewal records, beneficiary/caregiver contact logs, prior-authorization records, complaints, reversals, returns, and supplier/marketer identifiers. Join claims to beneficiary, supplier, HCPCS or product family, and order identifiers; sort each item episode by service date and compute for every refill: days since prior paid shipment, billed quantity, days' supply, estimated depletion date from prior quantity and utilization, days early or late relative to depletion, whether a qualifying request exists in the defined pre-dispensing window, whether the latest event is only a prescription renewal, and whether a death, hospice, admission, discontinuation, or return event precedes shipment. For each beneficiary-item-supplier episode with at least six cycles, calculate coefficient of variation of refill intervals, proportion of intervals within a narrow regularity band, proportion of near-maximum-quantity claims, early-refill rate, request-missing rate, post-stop-event rate, reversal/return/unopened-package/complaint rate, and continuation rate after therapy or equipment status changes. Produce a risk score using transparent weighted components: 25% missing-request rate, 20% post-stop-event rate, 15% refill-interval regularity, 15% early or near-depletion billing, 10% quantity regularity or maximum-quantity rate, and 15% adverse downstream outcomes. Aggregate scores by supplier, marketer, referral source, and product family using beneficiary-adjusted peer percentiles; flag episodes with high scores and suppliers in the top 1-5% of peer risk for manual request-record validation. Add a post-intervention change monitor that compares pre- and post-feedback distributions for interval variance, quantity variance, request documentation, reversals, and complaints, because a reduction in regularity without improved request evidence should remain high risk rather than being treated as remediation.

h21.minimum_viable_analytic: Build a monthly supplier-beneficiary-refill analytic using claims, authorization/order records, shipment and delivery records, beneficiary contact/request logs, provider and supplier master data, marketing or lead-source attribution where available, and beneficiary eligibility and geography data. Normalize HCPCS codes into supply categories and define an expected replacement interval and maximum quantity/frequency for each category. Join each refill claim to the most recent prior shipment for the same beneficiary, supply category, and supplier, then separately search a configurable lookback window for a beneficiary- or caregiver-initiated request linked to that shipment; retain request presence, request-to-claim days, request channel, caller relationship, identical timestamp indicators, billed units, days since shipment, and whether the beneficiary had documented DME ownership and medical necessity. Aggregate by supplier and rolling 90-day period: request-supported refill rate, percentage of claims within 5% of quantity or frequency limits, refill-interval coefficient of variation for beneficiaries with at least four cycles, duplicate-category claims across suppliers within the expected replacement interval, new-beneficiary growth rate, ordering-provider HHI, marketer HHI, and shared-provider or shared-marketer counts. Compute a supplier risk score using percentile ranks or standardized values for low request-supported rate, low interval variation, high limit proximity, high duplicate rate, high concentration, and rapid growth; require at least two independent indicators and a minimum claim or beneficiary volume before referral. At the beneficiary level, flag repeated claims where no request exists, the request timestamp is identical to other beneficiaries, the shipment interval is implausibly regular, or another supplier billed the same category during the replacement interval. Produce explainable outputs with supplier, ordering provider, marketer, beneficiary cohort, claim IDs, prior shipment, request evidence, feature values, and the rule contributions; validate against a manually reviewed sample and exclude documented exceptions such as authorized caregiver programs, institutional supply workflows, manufacturer replacement policies, and clinically justified early replacement.

h19.minimum_viable_analytic: Build a beneficiary-episode boundary-switching analytic using medical and pharmacy claims, DMEPOS claims, HHA episode and plan-of-care data, hospice election and revocation data, provider and supplier master files, referral/order data, diagnosis-to-terminal-condition mappings, and ownership or address affiliations. Normalize each claim to beneficiary, service date, HCPCS or product family, modifier, POS, billing NPI, rendering or ordering NPI, supplier, diagnosis group, units, rental or purchase status, and allowed amount. Join claims to HHA and hospice intervals using beneficiary ID and service-date overlap, then generate event windows from 14 days before through 14 days after HHA admission, HHA discharge, hospice election, hospice revocation, and material plan-of-care changes. For each beneficiary and event window compute: active-episode indicator; DMEPOS or supply claim count and allowed amount; proportion of claims during HHA or hospice intervals; exact and functional-equivalent overlap with HHA or hospice-covered items; HCPCS-family change; POS change; billing-entity change; ordering-clinician change; diagnosis relationship to the terminal condition; oxygen or DME exception documentation indicator; pre/post-event utilization ratio; same-item replacement or rental overlap; and supplier-to-beneficiary referral concentration. Produce a weighted anomaly score, for example 25% for functional-overlap or duplicate evidence, 20% for claims during an active bundled interval, 15% for abrupt HCPCS or POS change, 15% for entity or ordering-clinician change, 10% for terminal-condition billing without unrelated-condition support, 10% for abnormal pre/post-event timing, and 5% for network concentration. h06.minimum_viable_analytic: Build an episode-level analytic from adjudicated DME claims, reversals and adjustments, beneficiary eligibility, supplier/NPI and TIN data, HCPCS/modifier and rental-month indicators, equipment serial or asset identifiers when available, prescription and medical-necessity document metadata, and inpatient/SNF facility claims. Normalize claims to beneficiary-equipment keys using beneficiary ID plus HCPCS and clinically equivalent-code groups; use serial number, manufacturer asset ID, or supplier-reported equipment identifier as a stronger key when present. For each key, sort paid rental service months across all suppliers, collapse reversals, and assign a cumulative paid-month sequence while retaining supplier, claim date, modifier, and billed month. Join inpatient/SNF stays by beneficiary and test whether each claimed anniversary reset has a qualifying facility stay whose date range overlaps the prior anniversary date under the applicable rule. Compute features over rolling 12- and 24-month windows: paid rental months, maximum cumulative episode length, number of suppliers, supplier changes within 365 days, new KH or first-month indicators within 12 months of prior KJ or month-10/month-15 claims, days between the prior rental and restart, overlapping rental days, short-gap restart count, unsupported anniversary-reset count, percentage of months billed by multiple suppliers, and documentation-present indicators for purported resets. Assign an anomaly score using a weighted points model: 5 points for more than 15 paid rental months without a validated reset, 4 for any overlapping supplier rental, 4 for a new KH/first-month indicator within 12 months of a prior late-episode claim, 3 for a restart after less than 60 days without validated documentation, 4 for an unsupported anniversary shift, 2 for each additional supplier after the first, and 2 for each additional excess paid month; cap or winsorize extreme counts. Aggregate beneficiary-level scores to supplier, TIN, referral-source, and geographic-network levels using counts, rates per 1,000 episodes, and percentile ranks against peer suppliers. Produce two work queues: immediate prepayment review for active claims with score at least 5 or any overlap, and retrospective SIU review for suppliers in the top 1 percent of episode-level rates or with at least 10 affected beneficiaries. Exclude documented valid exceptions from the numerator after manual adjudication, retain them as labeled outcomes, and periodically recalibrate thresholds against confirmed improper-payment findings.

h04.minimum_viable_analytic: Build a beneficiary-month oxygen episode table from adjudicated claims, including claim and service dates, HCPCS/modifiers, units, allowed amount, supplier, ordering provider, place of service, rental-versus-purchase indicators, and denial or edit outcomes. Join each episode to durable-medical-equipment rental and purchase history, title or capped-rental completion records, prior authorizations, signed orders, oximetry or qualifying-test records, and CWF-equivalent portable-oxygen history using beneficiary ID plus service-date validity windows; join provider and supplier reference tables for specialty, geography, and enrollment status. Normalize each line into attributes: stationary present, portable present, contents present, ownership state, QF/QG/QB state, prescribed LPM, qualifying-test date, and whether a purchase or ownership event exists. For every beneficiary-month, derive mutually-exclusive-combination flags, QG/QB-to-portable claims within 30 days before or after, contents fees without qualifying rented or owned equipment, ownership transitions without a purchase/title event, separately paid portable equipment during an active QF/QB period, and LPM values near or above modifier thresholds. Aggregate these features by supplier and ordering provider over rolling 90-day and 12-month windows, computing rates per oxygen beneficiary-month, regional peer percentile or robust z-score, threshold-bunching statistics, new-beneficiary growth, and pre/post-edit changes. Produce a composite risk score using transparent weighted rules: for example, 30% mutually exclusive payment-path rate, 20% unsupported ownership transitions, 20% high-flow/portable timing conflicts, 15% contents-without-equipment rate, and 15% supplier or provider peer deviation; require minimum volume, suppress scores for sparse cells, and route the highest-scoring supplier-beneficiary clusters for medical-record and equipment-history validation. Retain line-level explanations for each score so investigators can distinguish documentation gaps from systematic billing behavior.

recommended_actions.action: Implement a beneficiary-HCPCS-family episode edit that carries the original rental start and anniversary date across supplier changes, rejects or pends a new KH or first-month rental claim when a prior episode exists, and caps cumulative paid rental months unless an approved interruption is documented.
recommended_actions.rationale: The core vulnerability is loss of longitudinal episode history when billing moves between NPIs. A payer-controlled episode ledger prevents supplier changes from resetting month counts or creating duplicate starts.

h22.minimum_viable_analytic: Build a monthly episode-ledger analytic using paid and denied Medicare claims, beneficiary enrollment and managed-care transition data, supplier NPI and enrollment data, HCPCS/modifier fields, dates of service, ordering and referring provider identifiers, place of service, delivery address, equipment serial or inventory identifiers where available, and transfer or ownership documentation. Normalize claims to a beneficiary-HCPCS-family key, with family mappings maintained by clinical and DME policy staff. For each key, sort paid rental claims by service month and retain supplier NPI, KH/KI/KJ status, units, allowed amount, and claim status. Start an episode at the earliest supported rental month; preserve the episode across supplier changes; increment the cumulative paid-month counter by distinct service month, while applying a policy table for qualifying interruptions and managed-care transitions rather than treating every gap as a reset. Join each claim to the immediately prior paid rental month and prior supplier, then compute: days since prior rental, supplier-change indicator, new-KH-after-prior-episode indicator, overlapping supplier-month indicator, cumulative paid rental months, months beyond the applicable cap, replacement months billed versus calculated remaining months, post-cap claim indicator, missing-transfer-documentation indicator, and whether the new supplier is linked to the prior supplier through shared beneficiary, ordering provider, delivery address, contact, equipment identifier, ownership, or banking attributes where legally available. Aggregate supplier and supplier-pair features over rolling 6-, 12-, and 24-month windows, including episode-reset rate, excess-month rate, overlap rate, post-cap rate, number of connected suppliers, shared-beneficiary count, and concentration of handoffs. Produce an explainable risk score using weighted rules: 5 points for any episode exceeding 15 paid rental months without a documented exception, 4 for a new KH or first-month rental within 60 days of a prior KJ or final rental claim, 4 for overlapping rental months, 3 for replacement months exceeding calculated remaining months, 3 for post-cap claims without ownership or servicing evidence, and 1-3 for network linkage and repeated behavior. Escalate episodes with a score of at least 5 and supplier clusters with high rates relative to peer suppliers, using minimum-volume thresholds and manual review for legitimate equipment replacement, beneficiary moves, payer transitions, or documented qualifying interruptions.

archetype_misuse_ranking.archetype: Organized fraud-ring archetype (cooperating suppliers, clinicians, marketers, beneficiaries)
archetype_misuse_ranking.why: Very high coordination (5), risk tolerance (5), access to beneficiaries (5), willingness to exploit ambiguity (5), and volume-growth objective (5) support deliberate cross-supplier episode fragmentation.

After payer feedback, activity would likely shift across additional suppliers or geographies while preserving the same episode-level anomalies.

archetype_misuse_ranking.archetype: DME supplier heavily dependent on lead-generation companies
archetype_misuse_ranking.why: High access to beneficiaries (5), geographic reach (5), coordination (5), volume-growth objective (5), and willingness to exploit ambiguity (4) create substantial handoff risk.
archetype_misuse_ranking.how: Claims would show large cohorts moving between marketer-connected suppliers with weak transfer documentation and frequent first-month rentals after recent supplier activity. After feedback, the pattern may become distributed across more NPIs, while shared leads, addresses, providers, or contact data remain observable.

archetype_misuse_ranking.archetype: Rapidly growing DME supplier
archetype_misuse_ranking.why: High volume-growth objective (5), risk tolerance (4), Medicare dependence (4), and willingness to exploit ambiguity (4) combine with limited compliance maturity (2).
archetype_misuse_ranking.how: The supplier would show a surge of new rental starts and replacement claims shortly after other suppliers' final rental months, with incomplete episode histories and excess-month exceptions. After payer scrutiny, growth and supplier handoffs may slow or shift to affiliated entities, but the episode and beneficiary overlap signals would persist.

archetype_misuse_ranking.archetype: Supplier with unusually high Medicare concentration
archetype_misuse_ranking.why: High Medicare dependence (5) creates strong financial incentive, but lower coordination (2), geographic reach (2), and volume-growth objective (3) limit networked misuse potential.
archetype_misuse_ranking.how: Claims may contain repeated supplier changes, post-cap rentals, or aggressive interpretation of anniversary and interruption rules within the supplier's own book of business. After feedback, billing may become more selective or documentation-focused, with fewer but still detectable episode exceptions.
